newsitem.title: SWEDEN: H&M doesn't see owners fleeing after move.
newsitem.headline: H&M doesn't see owners fleeing after move.

text.p: Swedish fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz said on Thursday it did not see institutional owners fleeing because of its decision to transfer its shares from the Stockholm bourse's main A list to the smaller O list.

"I have been in contact with about 10 Swedish institutional investors and of those only one has been outright negative to the decision to move the shares," Hennes & Mauritz Chairman Sten Wikander told Reuters.
"I'm not under the impression that they will step out of their ownership because of this."
Wikander said he also expected foreign institutional investors to stay on.
"We have asked an investment bank to contact our foreign owners and we are not under the impression that they will sell their stakes because of the move," he said.

The company announced earlier on Thursday it planned to move its shares as of June 10 following a new law, adopted last week, by which the owners of family-owned firms traded on the exchange's primary A list have to pay a higher wealth tax.

H&M's capital is about 38 percent owned by chief executive Stefan Persson and his family and the family controls about 70 percent of the voting rights. Persson's father founded the company which has been listed since 1974.

The group's shares tumbled on the news, plunging to 231 crowns from 257 crowns before the announcement. At 1330 GMT the share was changing hands at 230 crowns, down 24 crowns from its day earlier close.
"Overseas portfolio administrators cannot own O-listed shares without special permission," said one broker.
"Really it is only foreigners and Stefan Persson and family that own the company."
Wikander said the board had expected the share to fall but not this much.
"None of the owners have been particularly positive to the decision and we counted on a certain negative share price reaction," he said. "But we had not expected such a big downturn."
"A couple of the owners have said that they value Persson as owner more than the advantage of trading on the A list," Wikander said.
If the company had kept its shares on the A list, Persson could have been forced to sell part of his stake to pay the wealth tax, he said.
